items.title: Eighteenth century Yersinia pestis genomes reveal the long-term persistence of an historical plague focus
items.who: K. I. Bos, A. Herbig et al.
items.note: Genomes from the 1720–22 Marseille epidemic descend from Black Death strains, implying a persistent focus somewhere in or near Europe rather than fresh Asian introductions.

items.title: Yersinia pestis DNA identified in 1665 Great Plague burials at the Bedlam burial ground, London
items.who: Museum of London Archaeology and MPI for the Science of Human History
items.note: First molecular confirmation that London's last major epidemic was caused by Y. pestis, from teeth in a mass burial pit at Liverpool Street.

items.title: Navigable rivers facilitated the spread and recurrence of plague in pre-industrial Europe
items.who: R. P. H. Yue, H. F. Lee and C. Y. H. Wu
items.note: Spatial statistics on georeferenced outbreak records linking recurrence to river networks, part of a series on transport and plague persistence.

items.title: Plague and Lethal Epidemics in the Pre-Industrial World
items.who: G. Alfani and T. E. Murphy
items.note: Review of environmental and institutional factors shaping plague's spread and impact up to 1800, including the role of public-health institutions in its retreat.

items.title: Trade routes and plague transmission in pre-industrial Europe
items.who: R. P. H. Yue, H. F. Lee and C. Y. H. Wu
items.note: Tests the trade-route hypothesis against 6,656 georeferenced outbreaks and finds outbreaks clustered along major routes.

items.title: Dangers of Noncritical Use of Historical Plague Data
items.who: J. Roosen and D. R. Curtis
items.note: Warns that digitized outbreak lists derived from Biraben carry gaps and biases that can mislead climate and reintroduction models.

items.title: Human ectoparasites and the spread of plague in Europe during the Second Pandemic
items.who: K. R. Dean, F. Krauer et al.
items.note: Compartmental models fitted to nine outbreaks favour human fleas and lice over rats as the main vector, which would shift explanations for plague's end.

items.title: Phylogeography of the second plague pandemic revealed through analysis of historical Yersinia pestis genomes
items.who: M. A. Spyrou, M. Keller et al.
items.note: New genomes trace a single Black Death lineage diversifying in Europe, with a late branch persisting into the eighteenth century.

items.title: The Yellow Flag: Quarantine and the British Mediterranean World, 1780–1860
items.who: A. Chase-Levenson
items.note: Study of lazarettos and quarantine practice in Malta and the British Mediterranean during the long period without western European plague.

items.title: Biraben's lists of the plague epidemics of the second plague pandemic, 1346 – c. 1690: problems, basis, uses
items.who: O. J. Benedictow
items.note: Source-critical assessment of the outbreak inventory on which most quantitative work on plague's retreat depends.

items.title: Yersinia pestis strains from Latvia show depletion of the pla virulence gene at the end of the second plague pandemic
items.who: J. Susat, J. H. Bonczarowska et al.
items.note: Genomes from Latvia dating to the end of the second pandemic show reduced copy number of the pla virulence gene, an early sign of pathogen change.

items.title: A genomic and historical synthesis of plague in 18th century Eurasia
items.who: M. Guellil, O. Kersten et al.
items.note: Nine late second-pandemic genomes, including the first from the Caucasus, support introductions from reservoirs outside Europe rather than a European focus.

items.title: No particular genomic features underpin the dramatic economic consequences of 17th century plague epidemics in Italy
items.who: A. Seguin-Orlando, C. Costedoat et al.
items.note: Genomes from the 1630–31 Italian epidemic show no distinctive pathogen traits, pointing to social and ecological rather than bacterial causes of severity.

items.title: Perceptions of plague in eighteenth-century Europe
items.who: P. Slack
items.note: Compares the last great epidemics in Germany, France and Moscow and the official consensus that contagion and its control explained plague's retreat.

items.title: Palaeogenomic analysis of black rat (Rattus rattus) reveals multiple European introductions associated with human economic history
items.who: H. Yu, A. Jamieson, A. Hulme-Beaman et al.
items.note: Ancient rat genomes point to separate Roman and medieval introductions to Europe, giving direct data for the old rodent-replacement argument.

items.title: End of a Pandemic? Contemporary Explanations for the End of Plague in 18th-Century England
items.who: P. Slack
items.note: Examines how eighteenth-century English writers accounted for plague's absence, from providence and climate to quarantine.

items.title: The Great Plague Scare of 1720: Disaster and Diplomacy in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World
items.who: C. Ermus
items.note: Shows how the Provence epidemic triggered coordinated quarantine and cordon measures across Europe and the Atlantic, the policy response credited with containing it.

items.title: No evidence for persistent natural plague reservoirs in historical and modern Europe
items.who: N. C. Stenseth, Y. Tao, C. Zhang et al.
items.note: Ecological and outbreak analysis arguing Europe never held long-lived wild-rodent reservoirs, so plague's end depended on interrupted reintroduction.

items.title: Synergy-Plague: Reconstructing the environmental, biological, and societal drivers of plague outbreaks in Eurasia between 1300 and 1900 CE
items.who: University of Oslo (coordinator) et al.
items.note: ERC Synergy Grant (2024–2030, €8.38 million); one of its four questions is why plague disappeared from Europe and the Middle East in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

items.title: Attenuation of virulence in Yersinia pestis across three plague pandemics
items.who: R. K. Sidhu, M. Mas Fiol, P. Lê-Bury et al.
items.note: Finds pla copy-number depletion in late first- and second-pandemic strains and shows it lowers bubonic lethality in mice, a candidate biological factor in late-pandemic dynamics.
